concept.name: Feature Flags & Progressive Delivery

relationships.description: Connects Feature Flags & Progressive Delivery to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Feature flags decouple code deployment from feature release by wrapping runtime behavior in dynamic configuration predicates evaluated per user, tenant, or traffic percentage.
spark.keyTakeaway: By moving release control from git merges to sub-millisecond flag evaluation, teams gain instant kill switches, zero-downtime canary rollouts, and production A/B experimentation.

concept.whyItMatters: In traditional release cycles, shipping a buggy feature requires a full code revert, CI build, and container redeployment—taking 15–45 minutes while error rates spike. Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature) separate *deployment* (pushing binaries to production) from *release* (exposing behavior to users). Engineers merge incomplete work behind an `off` flag, test in production with internal employees, ramp traffic 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% while watching SLOs, and flip a kill switch in under 1 second if p99 latency or error budgets degrade.
whenToUse: High-risk infrastructure migrations (switching from Postgres to DynamoDB, testing a new ML ranking model, or rolling out a rewritten checkout flow).
Trunk-based development where teams merge daily to `main` without long-lived feature branches and merge conflicts.
Tiered SaaS entitlements, beta programs, and A/B experiments where different tenants or user cohorts receive distinct behaviors.
whenNotToUse: Permanent application configuration like database connection strings, port bindings, or static tax tables—use environment variables or config maps instead.
Deeply entangled core data-schema changes where two incompatible database formats cannot coexist cleanly without complex dual-write logic.
Leaving short-lived release flags in the codebase indefinitely after 100% rollout—accumulating dead branches creates exponential testing complexity.
keyPoints: Deployment vs. Release: Code ships dark (`false`) in production containers; business or SRE teams activate it independently via a control plane.
Local deterministic evaluation: SDKs stream flag rules (SSE/WebSockets) into in-memory caches and hash `(flagKey + userId) % 100` locally in <50 microseconds—never making a network call per request.
Sticky bucketing: Consistent hashing (MurmurHash3/SHA-1) ensures user `u_482` always lands in the same 5% cohort across requests and devices.
Kill-switch safety: Operational circuit-breaker flags let on-call shed expensive non-critical features (e.g., AI recommendations) during traffic spikes in <1 second.
Flag lifecycle hygiene: Every release flag needs an owner, an expiration date, and automated stale-flag PRs to remove dead `if/else` branches post-rollout.

examples.title: Zero-Downtime Search Engine Migration with Canary Flags
examples.scenario: An e-commerce platform migrated product search from Elasticsearch 7 to OpenSearch 2 with a new BM25+vector hybrid scorer. A big-bang DNS cutover risked breaking checkout if recall dropped.
examples.outcome: Using an OpenFeature-backed flag `search-v2-rollout`, they started at `dark-shadow` (mirroring 5% of queries asynchronously), progressed to 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% live traffic over 4 days, and caught a facet-aggregation bug at 10%—reverting to 0% in 400 ms without a deployment.

examples.title: Black Friday Load-Shedding Kill Switch
examples.scenario: During a 12x flash-sale traffic surge, a personalization microservice calling a GPU inference cluster hit 98% saturation, threatening to cascade timeouts to the cart service.
examples.outcome: On-call flipped the operational flag `enable-realtime-ml-recs` to `false`, falling back to cached trending items in Redis across 200+ pods within 800 ms and restoring checkout p99 latency from 2.4s to 110 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates long-lived branches and allows instant rollbacks without touching CI/CD.
tradeOffs.con: Every active boolean flag doubles the theoretical state space (`2^N` paths); 20 uncleaned flags create untestable interactions.

tradeOffs.factor: Local SDK Evaluation vs. Central Evaluation
tradeOffs.pro: In-memory rule evaluation runs in <0.1 ms with zero per-request network dependency and survives control-plane outages.
tradeOffs.con: Exposes targeting rules to client devices if used directly in browser/mobile apps; requires a Relay Proxy or server-side evaluation for sensitive rules.

tradeOffs.pro: Limits blast radius to 1% of users while validating real production telemetry.
tradeOffs.con: Users switching between `v1` and `v2` mid-session (if keyed by session instead of `user_id`) can experience jarring UI or state inconsistencies.

failureModes.name: Knight Capital-Style Stale Flag Reuse
failureModes.description: Reusing an old flag name (`new-router-v1`) years later activates dormant legacy code paths on servers that still hold stale binaries or configs, causing catastrophic behavior.
failureModes.mitigation: Never reuse flag keys; enforce unique immutable keys and delete flag definitions + code branches together within 30 days of 100% rollout.

failureModes.name: Control-Plane Outage Blocking Startup
failureModes.description: Services block boot or throw 500s on every request if the LaunchDarkly/Unleash SaaS endpoint is unreachable during startup.
failureModes.mitigation: Always supply hardcoded safe fallback defaults (`evaluateBoolean("flag", ctx, false)`), persist last-known rules to local disk/Redis, and deploy a local Relay Proxy.

failureModes.name: Untested Flag-Off Fallback Path
failureModes.description: Engineers test only the `true` path in staging; when an incident forces flipping the flag back to `false`, the legacy fallback crashes due to a schema change.
failureModes.mitigation: Run CI integration tests with both `flag=true` and `flag=false`, and periodically verify kill-switch rollbacks in staging.

failureModes.name: PII Leakage to Client-Side SDKs
failureModes.description: Sending the full targeting rule JSON (containing VIP customer emails or enterprise contract IDs) to a React frontend leaks confidential customer lists.
failureModes.mitigation: Evaluate sensitive targeting server-side or via an edge worker, returning only the resolved boolean/variant map to the browser.

commonMistakes: Making a synchronous HTTP call to the flag service on every incoming API request instead of evaluating cached rules in memory.
Using `Math.random() < 0.1` instead of deterministic hashing (`hash(flag + userId)`), causing users to flip-flop between variants on every page refresh.
Neglecting to tag logs and traces with active flag evaluations (`flag.checkout_v2=true`), making it impossible to correlate error spikes with a rollout.
Nesting 4+ feature flags inside the same function instead of isolating behind a clean Strategy/Interface boundary.
Treating temporary release flags as permanent entitlement flags without separating their governance and TTLs.

sections.content:
## The idea

Feature flags (also called feature toggles) replace compile-time branching with **runtime conditional routing** backed by an external control plane. Instead of keeping an unlaunched feature on a separate Git branch for weeks, developers merge it behind a named predicate (`isEnabled("new-pricing-engine", context)`).

Crucially, modern feature-flagging is **not** a database query per request. The control plane pushes a compact JSON ruleset over Server-Sent Events (SSE) or polling to an in-memory SDK inside each application instance. Evaluating a flag is a pure CPU operation (~10–50 microseconds) that hashes the user or tenant key against percentage buckets and targeting rules, falling back to a safe default if the control plane is unreachable.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a progressive rollout of `checkout-one-click` from 0% to 100% across a 50-pod Kubernetes cluster:

1. **Bootstrap & Stream**: On pod startup, the OpenFeature/LaunchDarkly SDK connects to a local Relay Proxy via SSE and downloads the 12 KB flag ruleset into memory (falling back to a bundled snapshot if the proxy is down).
2. **Context Construction**: When `POST /checkout` arrives for `user_id: "u_9182"` (`plan: "pro"`, `region: "in-west"`), the handler builds an evaluation context.
3. **Deterministic Bucketing**: The SDK checks explicit allowlists (`internal_qa`), then computes `MurmurHash3("checkout-one-click:u_9182") % 100000`. At a 5% rollout (threshold `5000`), hash `3412` evaluates to `true`, while `78210` evaluates to `false`.
4. **Telemetry & Auto-Rollback**: The request attaches `flag.checkout_one_click=true` to OpenTelemetry spans and Prometheus metrics. When Datadog/Grafana detects p99 latency jumping >25% on `flag=true` cohorts, an automated webhook sets the flag to `0%`, propagating via SSE to all 50 pods in <500 ms.

sections.content:
## Taxonomy of feature flags

Not all flags have the same lifespan or owner. Treating them identically leads to technical debt:

- **Release Toggles** (Days–Weeks): Short-lived flags hiding incomplete trunk code. Must be deleted as soon as rollout hits 100%.
- **Experiment / A/B Toggles** (Weeks): Multi-variate flags (`control`, `variant_a`, `variant_b`) that emit exposure events for statistical significance testing.
- **Ops / Kill Switches** (Long-lived): Circuit breakers that disable non-essential heavy features (recommendations, third-party enrichments) under load.
- **Permission / Entitlement Toggles** (Permanent): Plan-based gates (`tier == "enterprise"`) that belong in a billing/entitlements service rather than ad-hoc release flags.

## Delivery & evaluation strategies

| Strategy | Evaluation Latency | Blast Radius on Control-Plane Down | Best Use Case | Primary Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **In-Memory Streaming SDK (SSE)** | <50 µs | Zero (uses last cached rules) | Server-side microservices, APIs | Memory footprint if 10k+ flags |
| **Relay Proxy + Local Cache** | <50 µs (pods) / <5 ms (edge) | Zero (proxy caches in Redis/mem) | Large K8s fleets (>500 pods) | Extra proxy hop to operate |
| **Client-Side (Browser/Mobile)** | <1 ms | Uses localStorage/defaults | UI layouts, onboarding flows | Exposes targeting rules if unhashed |
| **Remote API Call per Request** | 10–50 ms | Total failure without fallback | Never for hot paths | Adds tail latency & availability coupling |

## Failure modes

- **Flag-Induced Memory Leak or Startup Hang**: Configuring `initTimeout=infinite` causes a service fleet to deadlock on boot during a flag vendor outage. Always cap init timeout (e.g., 2–3 seconds) and fall back to safe defaults.
- **Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) in Experiments**: Evaluating a flag *before* filtering out bots or unauthenticated redirects skews 50/50 experiment splits (e.g., 47/53), invalidating A/B test results.
- **Cross-Service Flag Drift**: Service A evaluates `new_schema=true` while Service B still sees `false` during a 500 ms propagation window, causing serialization errors unless payloads remain backward-compatible.

## Clean architecture and flag hygiene

Avoid scattering `if (flags.isEnabled("x"))` across 30 files. Instead, inject a **Flag Router** at a single seam (e.g., Spring `@Bean` factory or Strategy interface) so removing the flag later is deleting one class and one branch.

Use the **OpenFeature** vendor-neutral standard (`EvaluationClient`) so your business logic does not lock into a single vendor SDK, and automate flag retirement: file a Jira ticket automatically when a release flag has been at 100% for 14 days, and run static-analysis checks to fail builds referencing archived flags.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use local in-memory SDK evaluation (SSE/streaming + Relay Proxy)—never make synchronous HTTP flag calls per request.
- [ ] Provide explicit safe fallback defaults on every `evaluate()` call and cap SDK startup wait to <= 3 seconds.
- [ ] Use deterministic hashing (`flagKey + stableUserId`) for sticky percentage rollouts.
- [ ] Tag OpenTelemetry spans and error metrics with active flag variants to enable automated SLO rollbacks.
- [ ] Isolate flag checks behind Strategy/Factory seams rather than scattering `if/else` across business logic.
- [ ] Enforce a 30-day TTL and automated cleanup tickets for every short-lived release flag.

interviewProblems.title: Feature Flags & Progressive Delivery
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Feature Flags & Progressive Delivery. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Feature flags decouple code deployment from feature release by wrapping runtime behavior in dynamic configuration predicates evaluated per user, tenant, or traffic percentage.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: App Pod (In-Memory SDK) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with OTel / Experiment Store.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, OTel / Experiment Store experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Never reuse flag keys; enforce unique immutable keys and delete flag definitions + code branches together within 30 days of 100% rollout.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: By moving release control from git merges to sub-millisecond flag evaluation, teams gain instant kill switches, zero-downtime canary rollouts, and production A/B experimentation.
Avoid trap: Making a synchronous HTTP call to the flag service on every incoming API request instead of evaluating cached rules in memory.
Avoid trap: Using `Math.random() < 0.1` instead of deterministic hashing (`hash(flag + userId)`), causing users to flip-flop between variants on every page refresh.
When to reach for it: High-risk infrastructure migrations (switching from Postgres to DynamoDB, testing a new ML ranking model, or rolling out a rewritten checkout flow).
When to reach for it: Trunk-based development where teams merge daily to `main` without long-lived feature branches and merge conflicts.

putItTogether.title: Putting Feature Flags Release Together
putItTogether.summary: By moving release control from git merges to sub-millisecond flag evaluation, teams gain instant kill switches, zero-downtime canary rollouts, and production A/B experimentation.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Feature Flags Release before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using an OpenFeature-backed flag `search-v2-rollout`, they started at `dark-shadow` (mirroring 5% of queries asynchronously), progressed to 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% live traffic over 4 days, and caught a facet-aggregation bug at 10%—reverting to 0% in 400 ms without a deployment.
